title: The broken tusk
hook: the pen breaks mid-Mahabharata; he snaps his tusk to finish

segments.voice: Yesterday, the race around the world, and Ganesha circling his parents. Your line was the whole world is close. Who did you go around? Today, look closely at his face. One tusk is missing. Day twenty-six.

Count the tusks on a Ganesha statue. One whole. The other is snapped short, and often he's holding the broken piece in his hand. There's a story for that, and it's a writer's story. The sage Vyasa has a vast poem in his head, the Mahabharata. He needs someone to write it down as he speaks. He asks Ganesha. Ganesha says yes, on one condition: once I start, you can't stop. If you pause, I leave. Vyasa says fine, on one condition of my own: you can't write a single line until you understand it. And they begin. Then, somewhere in the middle, Ganesha's pen breaks.
screen: `COUNT THE TUSKS.` → `A VAST POEM IN HIS HEAD.` → `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND.` → `THE PEN BREAKS.`

segments.voice: He can't stop. That was his own rule. So, the story goes, he snaps off his own tusk, dips it in the ink, and keeps writing. That's why he's called Ekadanta: the one with one tusk. Now, a word about sources. The scribe story, Vyasa dictating and Ganesha writing, is told at the beginning of the Mahabharata in some versions of the text. The modern critical edition leaves that passage out. And the tusk as a pen is a later telling still; other Puranas explain the broken tusk in different ways, including a fight with the warrior-sage Parashurama. The tradition keeps all of them. So hold it as a story, not a record. And look at what it holds. First: the two conditions. Ganesha says, don't stop. Vyasa says, understand before you write. Tradition says Vyasa slipped in knotty verses to slow his scribe down and get a breath. Speed and understanding, keeping each other honest. Second: the tool breaks, and the work doesn't. Ganesha gives up something of his own, something permanent, so the work gets finished. He's the remover of obstacles, and in this story the obstacle is a broken pen, and the answer is himself. Half-finished things pile up. A letter. A course. A drawer. The story doesn't say it'll be easy. It says finish the thing, even if it costs you a tusk.
screen: `EKADANTA — ONE TUSK.` · `A STORY, NOT A RECORD.` · `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND FIRST.` · `THE TOOL BREAKS. THE WORK DOESN'T.` · then, large: `FINISH THE THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one small unfinished thing. Sit and breathe first. Let one unfinished thing come to mind, something small enough to finish today. An email half-written. A dish in the sink. A thank-you you never sent. Picture yourself finishing it, start to end. Notice what's been stopping you. When the bell rings, if you can, go and finish it. The bell holds the time.
The broken tusk. Ganesha as Ekadanta, the one-tusked, who in the story snapped his tusk to keep writing the Mahabharata.
Your line: finish the thing. Today, one small unfinished thing gets its last line, even if it costs you a little. Day twenty-six.

howItsDone: Ganesha is honored as a patron of writing and learning; some Hindus write a line honoring him at the top of a new notebook or account book before they begin.

fork.setup: you're Ganesha. your pen snaps mid-verse, and your own rule is that the writing never stops. what do you do?
options: stop and fetch a new pen.
snap off your tusk and keep writing.
ask Vyasa to pause just this once.
fork.reveal: the story says he snaps his tusk and writes on. the tool breaks; the work doesn't.

original.note: Sanskrit: one (eka) tooth or tusk (danta), one of Ganesha's names.

trapdoor: what you thought: a god with a chipped tooth.
what it means: Ekadanta gave up part of himself so the great poem could be finished.
what a scholar hears: the Ganesha-as-scribe passage is left out of the Mahabharata's critical edition; the tusk-as-pen detail is later still.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1 (the scribe passage, in the vulgate)

notes: Fresh editor pass (2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'the longest poem in the world', 'almost any image', 'days of it', 'everyone has a half-finished thing', and the manuscript-count claims ('many old manuscripts', 'many of the oldest manuscripts'), keeping only that the critical edition omits the passage; 'look at what it knows' (stock) reworded.
The Ganesha-scribe passage is found in the vulgate Adi Parva but excluded from the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute critical edition. Confirm phrasing.
Tusk-as-pen is from later popular tradition; the Parashurama fight is attributed to the Brahmanda Purana. Confirm attribution.
Vyasa inserting difficult verses to gain time: traditional; stated as 'tradition says'.
